notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: [א] וְעִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא בְּהִרְהוּר הַלֵּב בִּלְבָד, שֶׁהֲרֵי נִקְרָא בְּכָךְ ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ אֲפִילּוּ הָיָה מִקּוֹדֶם רָשָׁע גָּמוּר, כִּמְבוֹאָר [בְּקִידּוּשִׁין מט:]
notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Nasso §5): “in Ra’aya Mehemna:”teshuvah — tashuv heh to the vav; that the letter heh is the confession of words… and it is the breath that issues and enters in the mouth."" Exactly the se’if: viduy is a real and distinct mitzvah with its own standing — the heh of the Name — and precisely therefore it is not the thing that makes the teshuvah of the heart valid.Izhbitz-Radzin — the hidden heart and the public act (Beit Yaakov on Torah, Vayigash 1:2): Beit Yaakov distinguishes with unusual precision between a sin that has remained in thought and a sin that has emerged into public action. While the fault remains inward, he writes, it is easier to return and repair, because the matter has not yet become externally fixed; and since what occurred in thought is known only to Hashem, 'teshuvah ba-lev' is sufficient, 'she-ikar ha-teshuvah hu ba-lev' — the essence of teshuvah is in the heart. Once the sin has gone out into deed, however, an additional problem arises: the sinful act is visible to people, while the inward return is hidden from them, 'she-ein adam yode'a mah be-libbo shel chaveiro.' Beit Yaakov is not denying the efficacy of inward teshuvah before Heaven. Rather, he is separating two planes that R' Tzadok also separates throughout this se'if: the inner status known to the Knower of hearts, and the public/legal status that human beings can judge only through revealed conduct. This is an especially close Izhbitz parallel to R' Tzadok's explanation of why a man can become a 'tzaddik gamur' through a genuine thought of teshuvah even though the world may still require observable acts before restoring his credibility. The stronger claim is therefore also the more disciplined one: teshuvah is not made real by public performance, but neither does hidden inward change automatically erase the evidentiary consequences of a deed already visible in the world. The heart is decisive before Hashem; human institutions must still work with the revealed. That distinction preserves both the immediacy of teshuvah and the integrity of halachic judgment.

notes.body_html: Kiddushin 49b: One who betroths a woman “on condition that I am a [complete] tzaddik” — even if he is [known to be] wholly wicked, she is betrothed [from doubt], for perhaps he contemplated teshuvah in his mind [at that moment]. This is R’ Tzadok’s proof that the heart’s contemplation alone can, in an instant, confer the status of a complete tzaddik.Tanya — the heart can turn in an instant, yet the heart has many depths (Likkutei Amarim, ch. 29 §13): The Alter Rebbe writes, 'af she-kevar asah teshuvah nechonah, harei ikar ha-teshuvah ba-lev' — even after one has already made a proper teshuvah, the essence of teshuvah is in the heart — and immediately adds that the heart contains 'many aspects and levels,' varying according to the person, the time and the place. This is a useful complement to R' Tzadok's apparently radical use of Kiddushin 49b. The halachic status can indeed turn in one inward moment: if at this moment the man truly regrets and resolves not to return to his folly, Heaven knows that truth and he is no longer the same rasha he was a moment before. Yet the Tanya prevents us from flattening that moment into a claim that all subsequent avodah has become unnecessary. Precisely because the heart itself has many depths, a real teshuvah can be both complete in the sense relevant to the present moment and still capable of further deepening afterward. R' Tzadok's distinction between the essence of teshuvah and the additional fences required of a baal teshuvah fits this structure well. The resolve of the heart creates the present turn; the continuing work exposes and repairs deeper strata of that same heart so that the turn can remain stable when circumstances change. This also explains why a later relapse need not prove that the earlier teshuvah was false. A genuine inward level may have been reached and then later overwhelmed at another level. The Torah can therefore recognize the truth of the first moment without pretending that the yetzer has ceased to exist.

Avodah Zarah 17a: Elazar ben Durdaya, utterly sunk in sin, “placed his head between his knees and wept until his soul departed; and a bas kol went out and said, ‘Rabbi Elazar ben Durdaya is destined for the life of the World to Come.’” Rebbi wept: “there is one who acquires his World in many years, and one who acquires his World in a single hour” — the very power of the heart’s teshuvah described here, in which one wholehearted moment of return makes a “complete tzaddik.”

notes.body_html: Bamidbar 5:7 (the mitzvah of confession): “וְהִתְוַדּוּ אֶת חַטָּאתָם אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ, וְהֵשִׁיב אֶת אֲשָׁמוֹ בְּרֹאשׁוֹ, וַחֲמִישִׁתוֹ יֹסֵף עָלָיו, וְנָתַן לַאֲשֶׁר אָשַׁם לוֹ” — “and they shall confess their sin that they did, and he shall restore his guilt in its principal, add its fifth to it, and give it to the one against whom he was guilty.” Meforshim: the Rambam (Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1) takes this verse as the Torah’s source for the mitzvah of viduy — verbal confession before Hashem. R’ Tzadok’s use: the verbal confession, “though a positive Torah commandment… is a mitzvah in its own right, and does not hold up the teshuvah, whose essence is in the heart alone”; note, too, that the verse itself joins confession to “restoring the theft” — the very case of the thief that the se’if goes on to treat.

notes.body_html: Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 38:31: “‘On condition that I am a tzaddik’ — even a wholly wicked man — she is betrothed [from doubt], lest he contemplated teshuvah.” Chelkas Mechokek (there): even though we still see the theft in his hand, and he is not [yet] called a baal teshuvah until he “casts the vermin from his hand” [returns it], nonetheless, since he resolved in his mind to return it, he is also called a “tzaddik,” and out of the doubt of betrothal she is not released [without a get]. Beis Shmuel cites the dispute whether contemplation helps for a robber before he has returned the theft, concluding that if he states he is contemplating teshuvah he is believed.Shelah — inward bittul is the essence, while speech and deed complete the cleansing (Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Bo, Derekh Chayim §4): The Shelah uses bedikas chametz as an extended map of teshuvah. Each limb must be searched in the place where 'chametz' can enter — the mouth for harmful speech and forbidden food, the eyes for improper sight, the heart for evil thought, the head for haughtiness, and so forth — but he then states the governing point: 've-ikar ha-bittul ba-lev, she-ya'aseh teshuvah be-khol libbo' — the essential nullification is in the heart, that he repent with his whole heart, with 'a broken and crushed heart.' He immediately adds that Chazal also instituted verbal bittul, so that the purification should extend through 'speech, thought and deed.' This is exactly the balance required by R' Tzadok's se'if. The heart is not merely one component among three; it is the root-act that makes the return teshuvah. Yet because the human being is a whole embodied person, a heart that has truly turned seeks expression through the mouth and limbs. Viduy and altered conduct therefore do not manufacture an otherwise nonexistent teshuvah, but reveal and carry outward what has already occurred at the root. The Shelah's chametz image also clarifies why R' Tzadok allows a man to be genuinely righteous at the moment of inward return while still requiring special safeguards afterward. One may have performed the essential bittul in the heart and nevertheless still need to search the many rooms through which old habits can re-enter. The root has changed; the house must now be brought into conformity with its new master.

notes.body_html: Berachos 5b: Four hundred jars of Rav Huna’s wine turned to vinegar. The Sages hinted that he had withheld from his sharecropper the [customary] share of vine-cuttings; Rav Huna accepted upon himself to give it — whereupon (say some) the vinegar turned back to wine, or (say others) the price of vinegar rose to that of wine. This shows that the acceptance to make restitution already effects the turnaround, before any deed.Chassidic parallel — the difference between inner teshuvah and merely imitating a tzaddik's practices (Maor VaShemesh, Ki Teitzei §13): The Maor VaShemesh attacks the assumption that fasting, self-denial, or copied devotional practices are themselves the essence of repentance. Teshuvah, he argues, is among the realities that preceded the created world; it therefore cannot be identified with an external act belonging only to the world of action. 'Ela bevadai she-ikar ha-teshuvah be-lev nishbar ve-nidkeh' — rather, certainly the essence of teshuvah is in a broken and crushed heart — 'be-chochmah u-ve-binah,' through understanding the greatness of the Creator and breaking the heart before Him. The fasts and disciplines are, in his words, secondary instruments that may help a person arrive at such a heart. He adds an important criterion: when the return is made through 'binas ha-lev,' it has endurance; when one merely copies what a tzaddik did without the tzaddik's daas and inwardness, the practice can disappear as soon as the spiritual weather changes. This complements R' Tzadok's distinction between the immediate reality of teshuvah and the later disciplines of the baal teshuvah. An inward turn is not 'less real' because it precedes visible action; it is more fundamental. But the authenticity of that inward turn is not measured by theatrical severity either. It is measured by whether the person's will has actually changed. Thus the Maor VaShemesh gives a Chassidic language for R' Tzadok's halachic insistence: teshuvah can occur in the heart alone, while the lasting transformation of habit and circumstance remains a subsequent task.

'Ela bevadai she-ikar ha-teshuvah be-lev nishbar ve-nidkeh' — rather, certainly the essence of teshuvah is in a broken and crushed heart — 'be-chochmah u-ve-binah,' through understanding the greatness of the Creator and breaking the heart before Him. The fasts and disciplines are, in his words, secondary instruments that may help a person arrive at such a heart. He adds an important criterion: when the return is made through 'binas ha-lev,' it has endurance; when one merely copies what a tzaddik did without the tzaddik's daas and inwardness, the practice can disappear as soon as the spiritual weather changes. This complements R' Tzadok's distinction between the immediate reality of teshuvah and the later disciplines of the baal teshuvah. An inward turn is not 'less real' because it precedes visible action; it is more fundamental. But the authenticity of that inward turn is not measured by theatrical severity either. It is measured by whether the person's will has actually changed. notes.body_html: Hoshea 14:4: “אַשּׁוּר לֹא יוֹשִׁיעֵנוּ, עַל סוּס לֹא נִרְכָּב, וְלֹא נֹאמַר עוֹד אֱלֹהֵינוּ לְמַעֲשֵׂה יָדֵינוּ, אֲשֶׁר בְּךָ יְרֻחַם יָתוֹם” — “Assyria shall not save us, we will not ride upon horses, nor will we say any more ‘our god’ to the work of our hands — for in You the orphan finds mercy.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — part of the prophet’s teshuvah-charge (Hoshea 14, “Return, O Israel”): Israel renounce their false supports and their idols. R’ Tzadok’s use: he reads “we will no longer say” as a clarified certainty — that this will not again be said or done; and this is the sense of the Rambam’s “and the Knower of secrets will testify” — not a precondition of the teshuvah, but that the sincerity of the present resolve be made clear.Chassidic clarification of Rambam's knowledge/free-will problem — Be'er Mayim Chaim, Bereshit 3:5:3: The Be'er Mayim Chaim states the paradox in almost the same terms as this se'if: 'vadai sheneihem emes' — both are certainly true. Hashem sees to the end of all generations and knows which road a person will choose, yet 'ein ha-yedi'ah zo machrachat ha-adam' — that knowledge does not compel the person — and human choice remains free. He applies the point to Adam and Chavah in a way that is especially relevant to R' Tzadok's discussion of the Rambam. The serpent's sophistry was to reason from the truth of free choice that they could safely expose themselves to a forbidden test: since Divine foreknowledge does not force them, they could choose well even after eating. The Be'er Mayim Chaim rejects that move sharply. Divine knowledge can truthfully know that a present resolve is genuine without converting the future into coercion. The penitent's obligation remains located in his present choice: at the moment of teshuvah he must abandon the sin without reserving an intention to return to it. What happens later belongs again to the arena of bechirah. Thus 'yedi'ah u-vechirah sheneihem emes' supports R' Tzadok's reading precisely because it refuses both errors — neither making Divine knowledge fictitious nor making human responsibility unreal.

notes.body_html: R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Beshalach §7): “the time for [rectifying] the blemish of the bris is on Shabbos… and they can rectify the blemish — and if all Israel should merit this, they are immediately redeemed; and the essence of the rectification is when he contemplates teshuvah” Exactly the se’if: what is being testified to is the state of the mind at this moment — “the essence of the rectification is when he contemplates” — and not a guarantee about a future that has not occurred.Izhbitz on the narrow human share of choice — without weakening present responsibility (Mei HaShiloach I, Vayeilech §3): The Mei HaShiloach writes that David HaMelech knew deeply that, although bechirah is given into human hands, the portion of independent human action is 'davar mu'at ke-klippas ha-shum' — a small thing, like the skin of garlic — while in the deeper truth 'kol asher chafetz Hashem asah ba-shamayim u-va'aretz.' He connects this awareness to Shabbos and Shemittah: periods in which man is made to stop acting remind him that even when weekday labor resumes he may not say 'kochi ve-otzem yadi.' This is a fitting Izhbitz background to R' Tzadok's insistence that Divine knowledge and human choice are simultaneously true. The Izhbitzer is not using the hidden Divine perspective as a prospective excuse for sin. On the contrary, the whole teaching is designed to break self-attribution after action and to restore the person to dependence upon Hashem. In the present se'if the same distinction is crucial. Before and during the choice, a person must own the small but decisive point that is actually his: he must not keep an intention to sin again. Only after a choice has genuinely been made can the larger Divine frame be contemplated. Read this way, 'ke-klippas ha-shum' does not shrink responsibility; it identifies where responsibility truly sits. The human point may be narrow, but it is exactly the point at which teshuvah begins. Once that point turns, the whole person can be assisted and redirected from Above.

notes.body_html: Berachos 19a: “If you see a talmid chacham transgress by night, do not think ill of him by day, for he has surely repented.” R’ Tzadok stresses this means a complete teshuvah in the interim, not mere regret — and probes the limiting case of a scholar who is seen to relapse.Me'or Einayim — 'one who comes to purify is helped' means added daas is drawn after the initial arousal (Toldos §32): The Me'or Einayim explains 'ha-ba le-taher mesay'in lo' through the structure of daas. A person first makes an awakening from below; then, precisely because he has come to purify himself, Heaven draws to him an added daas 'me-olam ha-ta'anug' so that he will be strengthened in his avodah. The help is therefore not a substitute for the first movement of the person but a response to it. This matches R' Tzadok's answer to the apparent difficulty in this se'if. If a talmid chacham later falls again, one cannot reason backward that no help was given and therefore the prior teshuvah must have been false. The maxim describes a living sequence: first a real human turn, then assistance that expands the person's capacity; later, new concealment or a new trial can still occur and require a renewed awakening. The Me'or Einayim even describes daas as sometimes being withdrawn so that it can later return in greater measure. That Chassidic pattern gives conceptual room for what R' Tzadok is defending halachically — a genuine spiritual state at one time need not be invalidated by a different state at another time. The truth of the earlier return is judged at the moment in which the heart actually turned.

notes.body_html: Yoma 38b: “One who comes to purify himself is helped [from Heaven].” R’ Tzadok resolves the apparent objection: the “help” is granted at the very instant of coming to purify; a later relapse (permitted by Heaven as a test) does not retroactively cancel the genuine teshuvah of that instant.Izhbitz — human effort in the revealed area, Divine help in the hidden area (Mei HaShiloach II, Nitzavim §3): On 'ha-nistaros la-Hashem Elokeinu ve-ha-niglos lanu u-levaneinu,' the Mei HaShiloach warns a person not to declare himself already clarified merely because he can blame the atmosphere around him for what he feels. Instead, 'yishtadel ha-adam leva'er ha-ra mi-kirbo ve-livdok ad makom she-yado maga'as ba-niglos' — a person must strive to remove the evil from within himself and examine as far as his hand reaches in the revealed matters — 've-Hashem yitbarach ya'azor lo ba-nistaros' — and Hashem will help him in the hidden matters. This is perhaps the cleanest Izhbitz formulation of 'ha-ba le-taher mesay'in oso' for the present discussion. The person is not asked to control every hidden layer of psyche and circumstance before his teshuvah can count. He is asked to do honestly what lies within the reach of his revealed choice. Once he turns there, the hidden work is not abandoned; it becomes the arena of Divine assistance. That makes R' Tzadok's position both demanding and merciful. The thought of teshuvah is sufficient when it is true because the human being is judged on the point genuinely in his hand; but sincerity requires that he actually use that point rather than invoke hidden causes as an excuse. The later assistance belongs to Hashem, and a later test does not retroactively erase the earlier human act of turning.

notes.body_html: Kiddushin 40a: “Anyone to whom a matter of forbidden intercourse presented itself and who was saved from it — a miracle is performed for him, as it says, ‘mighty of strength, who do His word’ (Tehillim 103:20) — such as Rabbi Tzadok and his colleagues” (whose accounts of withstanding temptation follow there). Hence one who faces the trial and is saved is a “mighty one of strength,” secured against relapse.Kedushas Levi — why the baal teshuvah can stand higher without manufacturing a new test (Kedushat Levi, Bereshit §24): R. Levi Yitzchak explains the superiority of the baal teshuvah through the work of transforming darkness itself: the fallen sparks are raised through Torah and mitzvos, and when they return to their root their light is intensified, 'ke-yisron ha-or min ha-choshech.' He therefore invokes Chazal's teaching that 'in the place where baalei teshuvah stand' the completely righteous cannot stand, comparing it to a son who wandered far from his father and whose return produces an added delight. This sharpens R. Tzadok's use here of the person who actually withstood the recurring temptation. The advantage is not that sin or exposure to sin is intrinsically valuable; the advantage lies in the transformation of a darkness that already existed. A baal teshuvah has confronted an energy that once carried him away and has now redirected that same life toward Hashem. The 'gevurah' praised in Kiddushin is therefore the strength of conversion and return, not the pursuit of danger. In the language of this se'if, repeated resistance can establish the enduring name 'baal teshuvah' because it shows that the earlier force no longer governs him; Kedushas Levi supplies the inner mechanism — the very distance becomes material for a stronger attachment once it has genuinely been brought back to its source.

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 107a: “Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav: a person should never bring himself to a test [nisayon], for David king of Israel brought himself to a test and stumbled.” David had asked why we say “God of Abraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov” but not “God of David,” and was told, “they were tested by Me, and you have not been”; he asked to be tested — and fell in the matter of Bathsheba. This is the proof-text against a penitent’s courting temptation.Izhbitz-Radzin safeguard against courting a test — Sod Yesharim, Shabbos HaGadol 3:1: Sod Yesharim gives a remarkably explicit formulation of the distinction R' Tzadok is laboring to preserve here. A nisayon can indeed raise a person: 'mi-sibas nisayon nis'aleh madreigas ha-adam,' because through the concealment of the test one who stands in it can discover that Hashem was present even within the hester. Yet the sefer immediately insists that this truth is only retrospective. 'Ha-adam mi-tzido eino rashai le-hachnis atzmo be-nisayon' — from his own side a person is not permitted to place himself into a test — and this remains so 'even in a case where he would stand in the test.' That is why we pray 'al tevi'einu lo lidei nisayon': a person is not authorized to desire a spiritual ascent purchased by deliberately entering danger. Only 'after Hashem has brought a person into some test without his knowledge' should he understand that the trial can be for his elevation and refuse to rebel against it. This is an exceptionally exact Radzin complement to R' Tzadok's rejection of a literal requirement that the baal teshuvah recreate the scene of his sin. The same hidden-Providence doctrine that can reveal holiness within a test also forbids turning that doctrine into a prospective heter. The trial may be read as Divine after it has arrived from Above; it may not be manufactured below in order to prove one's righteousness. Thus the deepest Izhbitz language of hashgachah itself becomes the strongest protection of ordinary halachic responsibility.

notes.hebrew_phrase_excerpt: וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי דְּגַם בְּסֵפֶר כְּלִי יָקָר [רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת חוּקַת] כָּתַב כֵּן, וּפֵירֵשׁ בְּשֵׁם ״יֵשׁ מְפָרְשִׁים״ בָּזֶה מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין אֵין צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים יְכוֹלִין לַעֲמוֹד״
notes.body_html: Kli Yakar, Chukas: the baal teshuvah’s might must be shown “in the very place he sinned”; and “some interpret” thereby “in the place where baalei teshuvah stand, the wholly righteous cannot stand” — for the penitent must return to the place and circumstance of his sin, which is forbidden to a complete tzaddik (to whom seclusion and self-testing are barred). R’ Tzadok records this but declines to rule it as practical halachah.Baal Shem Tov — a safer explanation of 'where baalei teshuvah stand' (Baal Shem Tov, Nitzavim §6:1): A teaching recorded in the name of the Baal Shem Tov explains the higher standing of the baal teshuvah without requiring him to recreate the scene of sin. The baal teshuvah, it says, has already known the 'heat and enthusiasm' of transgression; when he returns and turns to Torah and mitzvos, he can perform them with an unusually intense warmth and desire because he already knows what powerful yearning feels like. The tzaddik who never entered that terrain does not possess that same experiential transformation. This provides an important contextual counterweight to the striking report R. Tzadok records here from Rav Yeiva and the Kli Yakar. The special power of the baal teshuvah can be understood as the redirection of an already-experienced force, not as permission to create a forbidden encounter in order to prove himself. That reading also fits R. Tzadok's own hesitation — 'tzarich iyun me'od ve-lo nitan le-iamer klal' as a practical rule — and his later move to David's use of permitted desire to break the yetzer. The Chassidic advantage of teshuvah is thus preserved in its strongest form while ordinary halachic responsibility remains intact: one transforms the fire one has already known; one does not light a new forbidden fire for the sake of extinguishing it.

notes.body_html: Sanhedrin 75a: a man’s mind is “not settled” [satisfied] by what is permitted him, but craves specifically what is forbidden — as “stolen waters are sweet” (Mishlei 9:17). Hence, R’ Tzadok notes, David’s parading of the permitted concubines was not a genuine “test” of his yetzer (which craves only the forbidden), but a way to provoke and break the evil inclination through the good.

notes.body_html: Berachos 5a (“rouse the good inclination against the evil”): “Reish Lakish said: One should always rouse [enrage] his good inclination against his evil inclination, as it says, ‘Tremble and do not sin’ (Tehillim 4:5); if he subdues it — good, and if not, let him engage in Torah… recite the Shema… remember the day of death.” Meforshim: Rashi — one wages war upon the yetzer by rousing the good inclination against it, with Torah, the Shema, and the thought of death as its weapons.
